result.title: SpireBench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Strategic Play of Agentic Models with Slay the Spire
result.summary: Agentic large language models now tackle complex tasks, yet strategic reasoning over long horizons is under-studied: most agentic benchmarks are short and episodic, and performance on long tasks is hard to dissect into stored knowledge, reasoning and luck. We introduce SpireBench, in which models play the complete commercial deck-builder Slay the Spire (StS), where early decisions decide long-term success. Across 20 large language models (LLMs) at the game's highest difficulty, frontier models beat heuristic baselines and match the average human player but remain far behind experts. This gap widens as the run lengthens: the strongest models win the first act as often as experts, then fall behind. What separates strong models from weak is how well they play each fight; all of them misjudge risk over a run, preserving health rather than spending it to grow stronger. A comprehensive, self-consistent renaming of every game term shows that part of their performance rests on prior knowledge of the game, and models do not improve from the memories they write across runs, which are often wrong and overly cautious. Our harness is the first to give a model the complete original game, and we compare it with existing harnesses. Overall, SpireBench offers an unsaturated long-horizon benchmark with tools to locate where and why agents fail.

AI.brief_summary: SpireBench 让 20 个 LLM 在最高难度下完整游玩卡牌构筑游戏 Slay the Spire，考察长时程策略决策，并分析其与人类专家的差距随流程拉长而变化、风险误判及跨局自写记忆无效等现象。
AI.relevance_reason: 其「长时程退化」「风险与资源权衡」「自写记忆错误」等诊断拆解，以及把表现归因于存储知识、推理与运气的思路，可能为 LVR 中的状态维持、停止/继续决策和贡献分配评价提供参照；但环境为纯文本游戏，与视觉 latent 推理联系较远，需核查是否可迁移。
